title: Code that checks code
objectives: See a test catch a broken change before it does damage
Write an assert that stops a script when a result is wrong
Choose test inputs whose answers you can work out by hand

screens.title: The file that flipped
screens.prose: Your script turns a vendor's closing prices into daily returns. It reads the file from top to bottom. This month the vendor switched the file to newest first, and told nobody.
screens.question: The script runs with no error. What does it report for this month's three prices?

options.why: You assumed the script knows the dates. It sees only the numbers, in the order the file gives them.

options.text: Nothing: it stops with an error
options.why: The script never reads the dates. Python divides any two prices without complaint.
You reversed the order but kept the sign. Going from £121.00 to £110.00 is a fall.

hints.text: Read this month's file from the top. Which price comes first?
The script pairs £121.00 with £110.00 first.

feedback.correct: A steady rise now reads as a steady slide.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pair the prices in the order this month's file lists them.

explain.text: The script paired £121.00 with £110.00, then £110.00 with £100.00. Both look like falls of about 9.09%. Nothing crashed, which is why nobody noticed.

screens.prose: You want a line of code that runs after the returns are computed and stops the script when they look wrong. Here are five candidates. Each one looks at `r`, the list of returns.

state.caption: `r` was `[0.1, 0.1]` last month. This month it is about `[-0.0909, -0.0909]`.

screens.question: Tap every check that would have stopped the script this month.

hints.text: For each check, ask: is it true for `[0.1, 0.1]`, and is it true for `[-0.0909, -0.0909]`?
Two checks look at a value that changed between the months.

feedback.correct: Those two look at something that changed: the sign, and the exact list.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the checks that are true last month and false this month.

byKey.only-exact: `r[0] > 0` catches it too. −0.0909 is not above zero.
byKey.only-sign: `r == [0.1, 0.1]` catches it too. This month's list is different, so the comparison is False.
byKey.r0c0: Reversing the file kept three prices, so `len(r)` is still 2.
byKey.r3c0: Both months give floats. The type did not change, only the values.
byKey.r4c0: −0.0909 is below 1 as well, so that check passes in both months.

explain.text: You kept the checks that are true last month and false this month. A check can catch a break only if the break changes what the check looks at. Length, type and a loose upper bound all survived the flip.

screens.prose: Each line you tapped is an **assert**: the word `assert`, then a condition. Here is one running on this month's returns.
screens.question: What happens when these three lines run?

options.text: It stops at line 2 with `AssertionError`, and line 3 never runs

options.why: You read `assert` as a kind of print. A false assert raises an error on that line.

options.text: It warns about line 2, then prints `returns saved`
options.why: You expected a warning. `assert` raises an error, so nothing after it runs.

options.text: Nothing happens: asserts only run inside a test tool
options.why: You thought `assert` needs a test runner. It is plain Python and runs anywhere.

hints.text: Is `r[0] > 0` true or false here?
Line 2 is where the condition is checked.
`r[0]` is −0.0909, so the condition is False. A false assert raises `AssertionError`.

feedback.correct: The false condition stops the script before anything is saved.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out whether the condition on line 2 is true.

explain.text: `r[0] > 0` is False, so line 2 raises `AssertionError` and line 3 never runs. When the condition is True, `assert` does nothing at all. That silence on success is what makes asserts cheap to leave in.

screens.prose:
The strongest checks compare a result with an answer you work out by hand. The function under test is `simple_return(p0, p1)`, the return from price `p0` to price `p1`.

```python
assert simple_return(250.00, 255.00) == ...
```

state.caption: Work out the return by hand

screens.question: What number belongs after `==`? Give it as a decimal.

hints.text: A return is the change divided by the starting price.
The change is in the third column.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the change by the starting price.

byKey.change: That is the change in pounds. A return divides it by the starting price.
byKey.later: You divided by the later price, £255.00. A return is measured from where it started.
byKey.ratio: That is `p1 / p0`. Subtract 1 to turn the ratio into a return.
byKey.percent: You gave a percentage. In code a 2% return is the decimal 0.02.

explain.text: £5.00 / £250.00 = 0.02. You worked it out without running the code, so the assert checks the code against something independent. Copying the code's own output into the assert would check nothing.

screens.prose:
A colleague's only check of `simple_return` passes:

```python
assert simple_return(1.00, 3.00) == 2.0
```

Then an edit breaks the function to `return p1 - p0`, with no division.
screens.question: Does the colleague's assert stop the broken version?

options.text: Yes: the formula changed, so the check fails
options.why: You expected the check to notice the code changed. It sees only one result, and dividing by 1 changes nothing.
Subtracting two floats is fine. The broken version runs quietly and returns 2.0.

hints.text: Compare the two results in the last column.
Dividing by 1 leaves a number as it is, so both versions return 2.0.

feedback.correct: The broken version returns 2.0 too, so the check passes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute what the broken version returns for these two prices.

byKey.changed: You expected the check to notice the code changed. A check sees only results, and here both versions give 2.0.

explain.text: Dividing by a starting price of 1 leaves the change as it is, so both versions agree. A passing check proves only that the code is right on that input. Choose inputs where the likely mistakes give different answers, such as £250.00 to £255.00.

screens.prose: `daily_returns(prices)` gives one return per gap between days. Three prices give two returns. What about a file with a single price, the day a stock lists?

state.caption: One closing price, the day a stock lists

screens.question: What should `daily_returns([100.00])` return, so an assert can pin it down?

options.why: You gave the single day a return of zero. A return needs two prices, so there is none to report.
`None` breaks any code that loops over the result. An empty list says there are no returns.
Nothing is divided. With one price there is no gap, so no division happens.

hints.text: How many gaps are there between days when there is one day?
Three prices have two gaps, two prices have one, one price has none. No gaps means no returns.

feedback.correct: No gaps, so no returns: an empty list.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the gaps between days.

explain.text: One price has no gap, so the list of returns is empty: `assert daily_returns([100.00]) == []`. This is an **edge case**, an input at the limit of what the code handles. Edge cases are where code most often breaks.

screens.prose:
Every useful check had the same shape: run the code on an input you chose, then assert the result equals an answer you worked out by hand.

```python
result = simple_return(250.00, 255.00)   # run the code
assert result == 0.02                    # compare with the hand answer
```

Code that checks other code like this is a **test**.
screens.question: Which line is a real test of `simple_return`?

options.why: You compared the code with itself. That passes whatever the code does.
That only checks the result is not zero. A wrong return of 10.0 would pass.
Printing shows a value but never stops anything. Someone has to read it and know the answer.

hints.text: A test needs an answer that does not come from the code itself.
Only one line compares the result with a number worked out by hand: £10.00 on £100.00 is 0.1.

feedback.correct: It compares the code with 0.1, worked out by hand.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for an assert against an answer worked out without the code.

explain.text: £10.00 on £100.00 is 0.1, worked out without the code. The self-comparison can never fail, and the bare assert accepts almost anything. A print checks nothing until a person reads it.

screens.prose: Put your checks in a function, so they can run again whenever the vendor sends a file. Write asserts inside `check_returns()` for `daily_returns`, with answers you work out by hand. Use round prices, such as £100.00 to £110.00, so each return is exact.
screens.question: Write `check_returns()` so it stops on a broken `daily_returns` and stays quiet on the right one.

widget.solution:
def daily_returns(prices):
    # one return per gap between days, measured from the day before
    return [(b - a) / a for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:])]


def check_returns():
    # Write asserts with answers you worked out by hand.
    assert daily_returns([100.00, 110.00, 121.00]) == [0.1, 0.1]
    assert daily_returns([100.00]) == []

tests.setup: daily_returns = lambda prices: [(b - a) / a for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:])]
daily_returns = lambda prices: [(b - a) / a for a, b in zip(prices[::-1], prices[::-1][1:])]
daily_returns = lambda prices: [(b - a) / b for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:])]
daily_returns = lambda prices: [b - a for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:])]
daily_returns = lambda prices: [(b - a) / a for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:-1])]
daily_returns = lambda prices: [0.0] + [(b - a) / a for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:])]

widget.how: Check calls your `check_returns()` six times. First with the right `daily_returns`, where it must finish quietly. Then with five broken versions in its place, where it must stop with an error.

hints.text: Choose three round prices, work out both returns by hand, and assert the whole list.
One broken version reads the list backwards, and one drops the last return. A steady rise and a check of the whole list catch both.
`assert daily_returns([100.00, 110.00, 121.00]) == [0.1, 0.1]` catches four of the five. Add the one-price edge case: `assert daily_returns([100.00]) == []`.

feedback.correct: Your checks pass on the right function and stop all five broken ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read which version your checks let through, then add an assert that tells it apart.

byKey.test-1: Your checks stop the right function too. Recheck one of your hand answers, and use round prices so each return is exact.
byKey.test-2: The version that reads the prices backwards got through. Use prices that rise, so reversing them turns the returns negative.
byKey.test-3: The version that divides by the later price got through. Check a return whose size you know, such as 0.1.
byKey.test-4: The version that forgets to divide got through. A starting price of 1 hides it: use £100.00.
byKey.test-5: The version that drops the last return got through. Compare the whole list, not one element.
byKey.test-6: The version that adds a return for the first day got through. Check the length, or the one-price case `[]`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped before the checks could run. Read the error under the editor.

explain.text:
A steady rise from £100.00 by 10% a day gives exact returns of 0.1, so `==` is safe here. Comparing the whole list catches the reversed, mis-divided and shortened versions at once. The one-price case `[]` catches the extra zero.

```python
assert daily_returns([100.00, 110.00, 121.00]) == [0.1, 0.1]
assert daily_returns([100.00]) == []
```

ideas: Wrong code often runs without an error. Only a check that knows the right answer can notice.
`assert condition` does nothing when the condition is true and raises `AssertionError` when it is false.
A test compares the code's result with an answer worked out by hand, on inputs where likely mistakes differ.

formula.name: The smallest test
formula.note: `expected` comes from your own working, never from the code.

summary.trap: A check can pass on broken code. With a starting price of 1, dividing and not dividing give the same answer.

quiz.prose:
```python
assert simple_return(100.00, 110.00) == 0.1
print("done")
```

`simple_return` is right, and this assert holds.
quiz.question: What does the script print?

options.why: You expected a passing assert to report itself. A true assert prints nothing.
A true assert is silent. Only a false one makes a sound, by raising an error.
The condition is True: £10.00 on £100.00 is 0.1. A true assert does nothing.

feedback.correct: A true assert is silent, so only `done` appears.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether the condition is true, then what `assert` does with a true condition.

explain.text: (110.00 − 100.00) / 100.00 is 0.1, so the condition is True and `assert` does nothing. The script carries on and prints `done`.

quiz.prose: A bug makes `simple_return` divide by the later price: `(p1 - p0) / p1`.
quiz.question: Which check stops the buggy version?

options.why: You picked a flat day. The change is zero, so both versions give 0.0.
Both versions return a float. The check looks at the type, which the bug does not change.
The buggy version gives about 0.0909, which is above zero too.

feedback.correct: The buggy version gives about 0.0909, not 0.1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what the buggy version returns for each check's prices.

explain.text: £10.00 divided by £110.00 is about 0.0909, which fails `== 0.1`. A flat day hides the bug because zero divided by anything is zero. Checks on type or sign pass for both versions.

quiz.prose: `daily_returns(prices)` gives one return per gap between days.
quiz.question: How many returns does `daily_returns([100.00, 110.00])` give?

feedback.correct: Two prices, one gap, one return: `[0.1]`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the gaps between the prices.

byKey.two: You counted the prices. A return needs a pair, so two prices give one.
byKey.zero: Zero is the one-price case. Two prices have one gap between them.

explain.text: One gap between two prices gives one return, `[0.1]`. One price gives none, `[]`, and $n$ prices give $n - 1$.
